Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary The end goal for this game is to be the player with the largest pile of wealth. The game is played over seven turns and on three different boards. The boards represent the same region over three different periods: the Age of Might, the Age of Faith, and the Age of Reason. There are 155 building tiles, in three colors. --Military buildings are orange. --Religious buildings are fuschia. --Civil buildings are blue. The following phases are played by each player during their turn. I. Exchange all or a part of your Construction Card hand. II. The Action Phase: 1. Travel in time. 2. Use Construction Cards to construct, demolish, upgrade, populate, or renovate a building. Note: certain buildings award an immediate Ecu bonus when they are constructed. III. Discard all remaining unused Construction Cards and draw 4 new ones. IV. Pocket Earnings from domains (only on turns 4 and 7). When a player finishes a game turn, the player to their left starts their own. When the turn comes back to the first player, the Turn Indicator pawn moves up a notch. I usually find games that others hate to be cool in one way or another but this wasn't one of them.  To be fair, there are cool concepts to the game (like the "ripple effect" into the other epoch boards) but not enough to make my gaming group want to play it again. [Rating: 1/10] 2-5 | (4) | 90 min | 10+ | Arnaud Urbon, Ludovic Vialla Khronos is a sort of 3D Tigris & Euphrates. Since I do not particularly enjoy the latter, my dislike for Khronos was a foregone conclusion. People who like spatial elements in a game might like it, though.

[Rating: 2/10] I don't like the fact tha you have to play on 3 board at the same time. The game is also short in amount of turns giving you little amount of time to play fully on all boards. I would have prefered playing only on 1 board. With 3 turns for each age so The game would end in 9 turns. Now you won't have any choice and play each age.

[Rating: 2/10] One of those rare "gems" that never even got played.  The rulebook was so bad that I knew I didn't dare spring it on my gaming groups.  I couldn't even get through my usual solitaire trial game where I work out a game's rules before teaching it to the gang...

[Rating: 2/10] Needlessly tedious, horribly time-consuming. The mechanics are intriguing and quite fresh but the result doesn't quite follow.

[Rating: 2/10] One of the very few games to bore me to tears. Unintuitive play, a theme that does not even make sense mechanically (why do I get more money for building in the Renaissance age? Why can't I even build in the modern age?), and various arbitrary rules made this a pain to sit through. To add insult to injury, the downtime is just ludicrous. When a game with seven turns takes two hours, there's a fifteen minute wait between turns, and that's a sign you're doing something wrong. A shame, because I adore all things time travel and really wanted to like this.

[Rating: 2/10] I so wanted to play this... Time travel! What's not to like? But as it turns out, I couldn't even sit through the rule-teaching. This terrible sense of dread and doom and "This seems just like Elasund" kept creeping up on me; and I finally decided I'd rather have bamboo slivers shoved under my fingernails than find out whether, indeed, it was. So I took my leave.   The players I quit on all liked/loved the game, so perhaps I missed out on something fantastic, but it just didn't feel like potential fun to me. [Rating: 2.5/10] Concept of having three "time zones" in which to effect changes and to have varying degrees of impact on the game was interesting, but the play is scattered and haphazard. I am not entirely sure why, but the game has failed to spark sufficient interest in me to play again.

[Rating: 3/10] File under "one trick pony".  The cool idea here -- events in the past rippling into the future -- loses a whole lot of coolness when you have to wait 20 minutes for your next turn, with little ability to plan ahead and even less to react while your opponents lay waste to your work and each other's.  The headache factor is increased by the rules of dominion and hierarchy (they're easy to forget), and you can barely do anything worthwhile if you get dealt all three colors, which can happen A LOT. [Rating: 3/10] I found this game very dull and boring. I can't think of much more to say than that. 1 Play.

[Rating: 3/10] Really seemed to be not very good after one play, but it's possible we were doing something wrong.  We thought it was overly fiddly and just more tedious than fun.  Pity, since I collect time travel games and I wanted to like this one in particular more than anything else in this years's Essen crop.

[Rating: 3/10] Difficult game to figure out from the rules. The one time on the table, we never could get started.  Rated low since I've never could get it played and never could break through the obtuse rules. Sold

[Rating: 3/10] "Hey, let's make a more ridiculously complicated version of Tigris and Euphrates!"  "Sounds great!  Let's make it slower and more dull!"

[Rating: 3/10] Didn't click with this at all! Far too much of a brain burner. Maybe bad cause 2p?

[Rating: 3/10] There are two main things I don't like about Khronos.  First, it reminds me too much of E&T, one of my least favorite games.  That's not a fault in design.  Rather, it's just a personal quirk.  Second, there is far too much downtime waiting for your turn.  I think this game lends itself to that even if the players are relatively fast.  Interesting concept though.

[Rating: 3/10] Ughhh.  a four might be too generous-but I might be talked into it again.....emphasis heavy on "might"  Dropped to a 3.

[Rating: 3/10] I really wish I could like this -- there are some interesting bits to the game but Tigris on 3 boards is still frustrating for me.  There was not much of a fun factor here, and I will actively avoid this game in the future.

[Rating: 3/10] There are too many rules and not nearly enough game to support them.  The box art suggests a wild and wacky time traveling adventure, but there's nothing wild, wacky, or adventurous about it.  By the end, I understood kind of what was going on, but only having four random cards in my hand severely limited me in being able to do anything to better my situation.  There was too much downtime, and not enough to do when it was my turn.  I had no fun whatsoever during this game.
